blocks.text: Context window optimization manages the model fixed maximum context capacity, deciding what actually deserves to occupy that limited space, distinct from token optimization, covered in the previous topic, which focuses on cost rather than this hard capacity constraint.

This topic covers prioritizing what belongs in the context window, truncation strategies once content exceeds the limit, sliding window and summarization approaches for long conversations, and how this connects to retrieval based context selection.
1. A Distinct Concern From Token Cost

blocks.alt: Building on token optimization, context window optimization manages a fixed capacity constraint

blocks.text: Token optimization, covered in the previous topic, is fundamentally about cost and efficiency, context window optimization is about a hard constraint, the model context window, covered in an earlier module, has a fixed maximum size, and everything relevant to a request genuinely has to fit within it or it simply will not be seen by the model at all.
2. The Fixed Capacity Constraint

blocks.alt: The context window is a fixed maximum size, everything must fit within it

blocks.text: Unlike cost, which scales gradually with token count, the context window is a hard cutoff, content that does not fit within it is not merely more expensive, it is simply unavailable to the model, this makes context window management a genuinely different kind of problem than pure cost optimization.
3. Prioritizing What Actually Belongs in the Window

blocks.alt: High priority, directly relevant content is distinguished from low priority, tangential content

blocks.text: When space in the context window is limited, not everything potentially relevant can be included, prioritizing content that is directly relevant to the actual current request over tangentially related material makes the best use of the available space.

blocks.text: 4. Truncation Strategies When Content Exceeds the Limit

blocks.alt: Content exceeding the limit gets handled by either dropping the earliest content or dropping the least relevant content

blocks.text: Two common truncation strategies exist when content genuinely does not fit, dropping the oldest content, keeping only the most recent material, or dropping the least relevant content regardless of age, which strategy fits better depends on whether recency or relevance matters more for the specific task.
5. Sliding Window and Summarization for Long Conversations

blocks.alt: A sliding window keeps only recent turns, summarized history compresses older turns

blocks.text: This connects directly to the earlier Memory Instructions topic, a sliding window approach keeps only the most recent conversation turns within context, while a summarization approach compresses older turns into a shorter summary that still preserves their key content, trading some detail for staying within the available space.

blocks.title: Summarization trades detail for space, sliding windows trade history for space
blocks.content: A sliding window loses older content entirely once it drops out, summarization keeps a compressed trace of it, choosing between them depends on whether losing early detail entirely is acceptable for the specific application.

blocks.text: 6. Retrieval Based Context Selection

blocks.alt: Stuffing an entire document into context is compared against including only the retrieved, relevant chunk

blocks.text: Rather than trying to fit an entire large document into the context window, retrieving only the specific, relevant portion of that document for a given request is a much more space efficient approach, this idea is covered in far greater depth in the later RAG Prompting module and the separate RAG and Vector Search course.
7. Testing Behavior as Context Approaches the Limit

blocks.alt: Testing behavior near the context limit reveals where degradation actually happens

blocks.text: Model behavior does not necessarily fail cleanly right at the exact context limit, testing with conversations and documents that push close to that limit reveals whether quality gradually degrades as available space tightens, useful information for deciding how much headroom an application should actually leave.
8. Context Window Optimization vs Token Optimization

These two topics address genuinely different constraints, token optimization, covered in the previous topic, optimizes for cost and efficiency, context window optimization optimizes for fitting within a hard capacity limit, a prompt can be token efficient while still poorly prioritized for context window space, and vice versa.
9. Building Context Window Awareness Into an Application

A mature application tracks how much of the context window a given request is actually using, and has an explicit strategy, truncation, summarization, or retrieval, for what happens as that usage approaches the limit, rather than discovering context overflow only when it starts causing failures in production.
Worked Example

A team building a long running customer support chat assistant finds that after enough conversation turns, the full history no longer fits within the model context window, causing the earliest, sometimes still relevant, details to silently disappear.

Implementing a summarization strategy, periodically compressing older conversation turns into a concise summary while keeping recent turns in full detail, keeps the total context within the available window while preserving key earlier details in compressed form, a meaningfully better outcome than simply dropping the oldest content entirely.
Common Mistakes

items: Not having any explicit strategy for what happens when content exceeds the context window, causing silent, unplanned truncation
Stuffing an entire large document into context when retrieving only the relevant portion would fit far more efficiently
Confusing context window optimization, a hard capacity constraint, with token optimization, which is about cost
Not testing behavior as context usage approaches the actual limit, missing gradual quality degradation

blocks.text: Practice

Take a long conversation or document handling scenario you have built or could build, decide explicitly between a sliding window, a summarization, or a retrieval based strategy for managing content that exceeds the context window, and test the chosen strategy against a genuinely long input.
Key Takeaway

Context window optimization manages the model fixed capacity constraint, distinct from token cost, prioritizing what genuinely belongs in a limited window and choosing an explicit strategy, truncation, sliding window, summarization, or retrieval, for content that does not fit, rather than allowing silent, unplanned data loss as context fills up.
